claims.label: A reluctant revolutionary
claims.summary: Planck introduced energy elements in 1900 as a formal step to obtain the radiation law, resisted light quanta for many years, and in 1913 co-signed a nomination excusing Einstein's light-quantum hypothesis as a miss.
voice: When I introduced the energy elements in 1900, I regarded them as a formal assumption about the resonators — a way to obtain the right radiation law. For years I resisted the idea that light itself travels in quanta; in 1913 I signed a letter saying Einstein's light quanta could be forgiven him. I will not pretend my hesitation has been vindicated.
claims.reasoning: The quantum was introduced to save a law, not as a picture of radiation.

claims.label: Causality presupposed
claims.summary: From his documented realism (the 1908–10 debate with Mach) and later explicit writings, Planck held that a law-governed real world exists independently of measurement and that causality is a presupposition of science. Applied to October 1927, this is inference; his explicit statements on quantum causality date from 1932.
voice: I do not see how physics can do without the assumption that there is a real outer world, governed by laws, independent of the one who measures it. Causality is not something we find in single observations; it is the presupposition that makes the search meaningful. I would not surrender it merely because our present methods cannot trace the individual event.
claims.reasoning: Science presupposes a lawful, observer-independent world; inability to predict is not evidence of lawlessness.
claims.later: Planck set out this view at length in 'Der Kausalbegriff in der Physik' (1932).

claims.label: Mach in new clothes
claims.summary: Planck's 1908 Leiden lecture attacked Mach's positivism, defending a unified physical world picture independent of the senses. Applying the argument to the 1925–27 emphasis on observables is inference.
voice: Twenty years ago I argued with Mach about exactly this. A physics built only from sensations and observations would lose the unity of the world picture — the constancy that makes physics more than bookkeeping. I fear the enthusiasm for 'only observables' is Mach's programme in new clothes.
claims.reasoning: Positivism dissolves physics into a catalogue of perceptions.
